title: Down to the Rafters
logline: In two days a thatched roof in a dry-zone village is taken down to its bare rafters, every strip of it carried off and burnt, and covered again course by course with plaited leaf cut this month, so that the same shot from the same height shows the roof, then no roof, then the roof.
human_question: When nothing that was there before is there now, on what grounds is it still the same thing?

place.what_kind_of_place: A dry-zone settlement village in the east: paddy in the low ground, thorn and jungle behind, a tank road, and homesteads set well apart under coconut, mango, tamarind and palmyra, each with a swept yard of red earth. The subject is one roof on one building — a long outbuilding, a cattle shelter, a kitchen wing or a verandah room — which is covered not in tile or sheet but in plaited leaf: coconut frond split down the rib and woven into flat strips, or coarse grass laid in bundles, tied course by course to a frame of round poles and split battens with strips of bark or cheap twine. Under the covering the frame is a thing in its own right and is meant to outlast many coverings: rough rafters with the bark still on them, smoked black underneath, notched and tied rather than nailed. Around the building, when the work is on, the ground becomes the workshop: fronds dragged in from the yard and the road edge, a bundle of them being split, a pile of finished strips, a heap of stripped old covering going grey and brittle, a ladder, a hook knife, a coil of twine, and a fire later in the week.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because the same frame, from the same height, produces three pictures that are the argument. From directly overhead the roof is a single textured plane, shingled in overlapping courses, dark where it is old and pale where the last patch went on. Strip it and the plane is gone: what is left is a skeleton of round poles in a geometry nobody ever sees, with the floor of the building visible between them and the whole interior open to the sky. Cover it again and the plane is back, uniform, pale, exactly where it was. The stripping itself is the most physically satisfying thing on screen: brittle grey material coming away in armfuls, dust and old nests and insects falling, the pole grid appearing a course at a time. And the re-laying is a craft at close range that does not need explaining — a frond split down its spine with one movement, the leaflets flicked over one another into a flat woven strip, the strip carried up a ladder and tied with three turns and a hitch, and the next one laid over its top edge so that water cannot find the tie.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Everything that can be seen, and nothing that matters. Between the first shot and the last, not one strip of the covering is the same object, and the building is in the same place, doing the same job, with the same name. In between there is a stretch of hours or a whole night in which the building has no roof at all and rain would go straight into it, which is the part of the work nobody chooses to prolong. The frame underneath changes only slowly, a pole at a time across decades, and it is the only continuous physical thing in the film. Across a longer time the practice itself is on a clock: the covering has to be redone every few years, and every renewal is also a decision not to put a sheet or a tile on instead, which would end the work and would be, for many households, an improvement.
place.when_it_looks_best: A dry spell, and one that is trusted to hold, because the work opens the building to the sky and nobody starts it under an uncertain sky. The overhead shots want the middle of the morning and the middle of the afternoon rather than dawn, because a low sun flattens the courses and a higher sun rakes across them and makes every overlap read. The stripping wants back-light and a little wind for the dust. The bare frame wants the middle of the day, when light comes straight down through the poles onto the floor. The re-laying is worth the last hour, when low sun comes in under the eaves and through the new covering from underneath. The whole thing is a two- or three-day job, and it cannot be filmed in a day.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A film about a roof being replaced by hand. Overhead, the covered plane; the first course pulled and the grey brittle stuff coming away in armfuls; dust, old nests, an emptied roof space; the pole frame appearing, smoke-blackened and notched; fronds dragged in and split down the rib in one movement; leaflets flicked over one another into flat strips; a stack of them growing; a ladder, three turns of twine and a hitch; course over course from the eaves up; the old covering burning in the yard; rain on the new one. It has a complete shape with nothing said over it: a covering, no covering, a covering. Anyone who likes competent hands, repetitive making, or the sight of a structure stripped to its bones has a whole piece here.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same three days become the sources' account of how one thing carries on as another, filmed on the one object where the claim is a matter of ordinary language. The books hold two ways of seeing at once: an unbroken continuity, like a seed becoming a shoot and then a tree, and a set of stages each with its own character and none identical to the last. Taken singly each becomes a mistake, and the text says which mistake and why. A roof with nothing of its old self left in it and the same name on it sits exactly between them. The voice never says the roof is a person and never asks anybody in the village what they think the roof is. It puts the question itself — on what grounds is this the same roof — and gives the sources' own answer: not the same, not something else, and nothing carried across.

sequence.on_screen: Mid-morning, from directly overhead. A single thatched plane among coconut and tamarind: overlapping courses running up to a ridge, dark and silvered where it is old, one paler patch where something was mended. Red earth yard, shadow of a tree across one corner.
sequence.voice: This covering is a few years old and is at the end of it. In two or three days all of it will be off and burnt and a new one will be on. The building underneath is older than anybody working on it, and after this it will be called the same thing it is called now.

sequence.on_screen: The stripping. Grey brittle material coming away in armfuls and going over the edge, dust in back-light, an old nest falling. A course at a time, the pole grid appearing from the eaves upward.
sequence.voice: The first of the four ways the sources tell you to look at this is continuity. The way a seed goes to shoot, to leaf, to stem, to branch, to tree, they say, a series runs on unbroken [C081-P:L523–L548]. Seen straight, that stops you thinking the thing was cut off and replaced by a stranger.

sequence.on_screen: The bare frame from directly overhead, at noon. Round poles with bark still on them, notched and tied, smoke-blackened underneath, the floor of the building visible between them in strips of hard light. No covering anywhere in frame.
sequence.voice: But the second way is difference: knowing each thing in the series by its own particular character, distinctly. Seen straight, that stops you thinking something unchanging has been running through the whole length of it [C081-P:L523–L548]. And the books are exact that each of these corrections, taken alone, breeds the error the other one was for.

sequence.on_screen: The yard. A frond split down its rib in one movement, leaflets flicked over one another into a flat woven strip, a stack of finished strips growing against a wall. All of it cut this month.
sequence.voice: Their argument for the middle position is not a mood, it is arithmetic. If cause and result were simply one and the same, then curd could not come out of milk. If they were simply separate things, then curd would have nothing to do with milk at all [C080-P:L955].

sequence.on_screen: A strip carried up a ladder and tied: three turns and a hitch, the next strip laid over its top edge so water cannot reach the tie. Hands doing it fast, and other hands doing it slowly, on the same course.
sequence.voice: They push it further. If it were absolute sameness, a man could never become anything other than a man; if it were absolute difference, the work one person had done could land on somebody else [C080-P:L957]. And their plainest picture for it is this: what a child was taught and practised shows up later in the grown body, and in nobody else's [C080-P:L961–L965].

sequence.on_screen: The finished roof from directly overhead, from the same position and at the same time of day as the first shot. Uniform, pale, every course new. The same tree's shadow across the same corner.
sequence.voice: So: is that the same roof. The sources will not have it either way. They say the result stands where it was produced and has gone nowhere; that nothing at all comes over from what went before; and that there is neither sameness nor difference here [C080-P:L945; C080-P:L929–L931]. Whatever this covering is, it is not last week's covering moved.

sequence.on_screen: The old covering burning in the yard, or lying in a heap going to nothing behind the building. Then the first rain on the new roof, from underneath, water finding its way down the outside of the courses.
sequence.voice: Two things the sources close off. Once something has given its result, it does not give it again [C080-P:L967–L969]. And the ageing of this new covering is not a judgement on it or on anybody: where there is birth, they say, ageing and breaking and drying follow, and where there is no birth they do not [C080-P:L1569]. The new roof began ageing the morning it went on.

sequence.on_screen: Last light. The building with its new covering, the ladder down, the yard swept, nobody in frame. Then the pole frame again in a still from three days ago, and the plane back over it.
sequence.voice: And the last of the four ways: from these conditions, these results and no others, the way milk gives curd [C081-P:L523–L548]. Nobody intended it. The sources are blunt about that: not-seeing does not decide to produce intention, and intention does not decide to produce awareness, and once you see that, there is no maker left to look for [C081-P:L541–L545].

concept_merge.why_together: C081 supplies the structure of the argument and C080 supplies its evidence, and the footage happens to carry both at once. The Pradeepika sets out four ways of seeing the round, and it is unusually careful about them: the method of identity is the unbroken running-on of a series, illustrated by a seed going to shoot, leaf, stem, branch and tree, and seen rightly it abandons annihilationism while seen wrongly it hardens into eternalism; the method of diversity is knowing each factor by its own particular character, and seen rightly it abandons eternalism while seen wrongly it hardens into annihilationism; the method of non-agency is that not-seeing does not intend to produce intention, and seen rightly it abandons the view of a self by understanding that there is no maker such as a supreme god; and the method of 'such is its nature' is that from milk come curd and the rest, and from these conditions these results and no others [C081-P:L523–L548; C081-P:L541–L545]. C080 supplies what the continuity is actually made of, and it argues rather than asserts: the result stands where it was produced and has gone nowhere, offered through an echo, a lamp, a seal and a reflection [C080-P:L945]; there is no travelling from the earlier existence and no passing over of anybody [C080-P:L929–L931]; if the two were simply identical, curd could not arise from milk, and if simply different, curd would have no relation to milk, with seed and shoot given as the same case [C080-P:L955]; absolute sameness would stop a man becoming anything else and absolute difference would let one person's work land on another [C080-P:L957]; the plainest image of all is a skill practised in childhood appearing later in the grown body and in nobody else's [C080-P:L961–L965]; and what has given its result does not give it again [C080-P:L967–L969]. A roof taken to bare poles and rebuilt out of leaf cut this month is the one object where all of that is a plain question about a plain thing, and where the answer can be tested by putting the camera in the same place three times.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the difficult middle position is not a paradox but a description of the only kind of continuity there has ever been, and that it takes work to keep both halves of it in view. Said flat, 'neither the same nor different' sounds like a riddle. Filmed as a covering, a skeleton and a covering from one fixed overhead position, it becomes a question a viewer asks before the voice does. The pairing also gives the film its guard rails for free: because C081's methods come with their misreadings attached, the voice can state the continuity and immediately state what the continuity is not, and because C080 refuses transfer in as many words, the film can stand on the most soul-shaped image in the group without implying a soul. The previous version of this idea made a household the subject and rested the claim on the family's own words about their house. That is dropped. A family's ordinary sentence about their own roof should not be made to carry a doctrine it was not making, and the film does not need it: the question belongs to the voice, and the evidence is the frame.

concept_links.why: The digest's four methods are the film's spine and three of them are narrated in the source's own terms, each over the footage that shows it. Identity is spoken over the stripping, with the seed-to-tree series the source itself uses, and with its stated function, that seen straight it prevents the view that the thing was cut off [C081-P:L523–L548]. Diversity is spoken over the bare frame, with its stated function of preventing the view that something unchanging runs through, and with the digest's structural point that each corrective produces the opposite error when taken alone [C081-P:L523–L548]. 'Such is its nature' closes the film in its own words, from these conditions these results and no others, like milk and curd [C081-P:L523–L548]. And non-agency is spoken last, in the source's own formulation that not-seeing does not intend to produce intention and that seeing this rightly means understanding there is no maker [C081-P:L541–L545]. Every limit in the digest is honoured. 'My soul is reborn' is the reading this footage invites and it is refused explicitly in the sixth beat. 'Life is a beautiful circle' is refused by construction: the film contains no circle, celebrates nothing, and its penultimate beat is about a heap of dead material and the new covering already ageing. 'What goes around comes around' as cosmic justice is refused by the closing beat, which is the digest's non-agency line and nothing else. The claim that not-seeing is an origin is avoided, since the film makes no claim about beginnings anywhere. The three periods, the four groups, the twenty modes and the two roots are not narrated: they are a diagram and this film has footage. Past-life psychology is nowhere in it.

This concept supplies the film's four narrated arguments and its two closing limits, and every one of them is anchored to what is on screen. The milk-and-curd argument is spoken over new material being made, because that is the moment the film is manufacturing a cause [C080-P:L955]. Its extension, that absolute sameness would stop a man becoming anything else and absolute difference would let one person's work land on another, is spoken over the tying, where fast hands and slow hands work the same course [C080-P:L957]. The skill-in-the-hands image is spoken there too and named out loud as the source's own plainest picture, not the film's [C080-P:L961–L965]. The refusal of transfer, with the echo, lamp, seal and reflection and the statement that the result stands where it was produced, carries the beat that puts the camera back in the first shot's position [C080-P:L945; C080-P:L929–L931]. The two closing limits are the digest's sharpest: that what has given its result does not give it again [C080-P:L967–L969], and that ageing and breaking follow on birth itself rather than being a verdict on anyone [C080-P:L1569]. Every limit in the digest that bears on this film is honoured. The warm slogan is refused, and the group's own title is not permitted to be the film's claim: nothing in this film is celebrated and nothing is described as a belonging. Rebirth as a soul entering a body is refused out loud. 'What goes around comes around' is refused by naming the no-repeat clause without any suggestion of payback, and 'you create your own reality' is refused by the absence of any agent in the film's account of the work. Ignorance is never glossed as lack of schooling; the term is used only as not-seeing, in the closing beat, and is not explained. The cosmology, the death-moment passages, the hells and heavens and the account of what a dying mind takes as its object are not narrated, alluded to or implied: nothing in this film stands for a death, the old covering is material and is filmed as material, and no household's loss appears anywhere. The prosperity and merit material is unused.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That a thing can be continuous with what came before it while containing nothing of it, that the tradition insists on holding continuity and difference together because each on its own becomes a mistake, that it gives an argument for that middle position rather than asking for assent, and that nothing intends any of it. The roof is an everyday picture of continuity without a traveller and the film says so; nothing here stands for a person, a death or anybody's deserving, and no household's words are used to make a doctrinal claim.
what_must_be_real: A renewal the building's people were going to do anyway, in the week they were going to do it, at their own pace. No covering is stripped early, kept on longer, or partly re-laid so that a shot can be repeated; no course is undone and redone; and no bare frame is left open one hour longer than the work requires, since an open roof is a real exposure and not a visual opportunity. Nobody is asked to say that it is the same roof, or asked what they think about identity, continuity or anything doctrinal, and no sentence anybody says about their own building is edited into an answer to the film's question. The people doing the work are filmed as people working and are not made into characters, exemplars or bearers of tradition. If the household would rather have a sheet or tile roof and is renewing this one for want of money, that is their business and is not put on screen as a virtue. Nothing about the building's interior, its contents or its occupants' circumstances is filmed.
position_hint: middle to late, after the group's crossing film and before its films about support at one moment. It takes continuity across a minute and stretches it across years, and it is the group's clearest place to state the four ways of looking with their misreadings attached, which every later film in the group relies on having been said once. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Letting the roof read as a soul passing on, which is the exact view the sources reject and which a replaced covering invites more than any other object here.
Sliding into the warm reading of the group's title, so that a description of continuity becomes a celebration of belonging.
Loading a household's ordinary words about their own building with a meaning they were not making, which is what the previous version of this idea did and why the household was dropped as subject.
Treating the work as picturesque, or implying that hand-laid thatch is better for the people under it than the alternative they may want.
Turning the stripped frame into a corpse or the burning heap into a death, which would put a person's ending on screen by implication.
Letting the film read as a lament for a dying craft, which is a real subject and is not this concept.
Prolonging the open-roof stretch, or filming in a way that encourages anybody to leave a building exposed for the camera.
Stating the continuity without immediately stating its misreading, which is the one thing the source is careful about and the easiest thing to cut.
drop_if: No renewal falls inside the filming window, so the stripping and re-laying would have to be arranged.
The work can only be filmed by asking for it to be done earlier, slower, differently or twice.
Whole coverings are no longer stripped and replaced here, only patched, so the bare-frame shot that the film turns on does not exist.
Height directly over the roof cannot be obtained, so the three matching overhead shots that carry the argument cannot be made.
The only buildings available are dwellings whose interiors and occupants cannot be kept out of frame.

connections.note: Two films on continuity with nothing carried across, at two scales: one arrival that takes a minute on a line somebody else strung, and one covering wholly replaced across three days.

A thing that holds across years by being wholly replaced is followed by a thing that holds for one instant because its parts lean on each other, which is a different kind of support and is only one of twenty-four.

selection.reason: The concept is a plain question about a plain object, and the answer is a camera put in the same place three times: covering, bare frame, covering.

review.note: Rewritten 2026-09-24 into the footage-led shape. What was dropped: the household as subject, the family's own testimony that it is the same roof, the teaching-and-inheritance thread about younger hands taking the skill on, and the stake about whether they will keep doing it this way. The family's sentence about their own building was being made to carry a doctrine it was not making, which is the one thing the concept's own digest warns against; and the passing-on thread duplicated the source's skill image, which the voice can name once as the source's picture without building a film on a household. The concept is unchanged and is now carried by the roof and the work alone, with the same-roof claim put as the voice's question. The merger flag against the crossing idea is also removed: that idea stands on its own and keeps this concept's rope image, which this film does not use, so the two no longer overlap. Both digests were re-read from scratch and every citation was verified line by line against the source files; the old idea carried no citations at all. The four ways of looking are narrated with their misreadings attached, because the digest is explicit that each corrective produces the opposite error if taken alone, and the closing beat carries non-agency rather than anything warm.

suggested_location.name: The leaf-thatched outbuildings of the settlement villages around Uhana, Ampara District

also_known_as.name: cadjan
also_known_as.meaning: the flat woven strip made by splitting a coconut frond down the rib and plaiting the leaflets over one another; the standard covering and walling material of the belt
also_known_as.used_by: general usage in Sri Lanka and across south Asia

also_known_as.name: gok-kola / pol-athu weeling
also_known_as.meaning: the plaiting of the frond into courses for a roof, as against its use for walls or fences

also_known_as.name: iluk / mana
also_known_as.meaning: the coarse grasses used in the same way where frond is short, laid in bundles rather than plaited

suggested_location.region: Ampara District, Eastern Province: the dry-zone settlement belt in the paddy and jungle country a few kilometres north of the district town, on the road towards the inland tank villages
suggested_location.why_here: Because the belt is full of buildings whose coverings are still whole-stripped and re-laid rather than patched, and because the surroundings give the film its overhead shot. The homesteads sit well apart in swept yards under coconut, mango and tamarind, with paddy on one side and thorn jungle on the other, so a single thatched plane can be isolated from directly above with nothing else in the frame, which is what the film's whole argument depends on. The material is grown where it is used: the frond comes off trees in the yard and along the road edge, is split and plaited on the ground beside the building, and goes up the same week, so the film can show the new covering being made out of this month's leaf rather than arriving from anywhere. The dry-zone rainfall pattern gives long reliable dry stretches in which a building can be safely opened to the sky, which is the one condition the work requires. And the subject can be an outbuilding, a cattle shelter or a kitchen wing rather than a dwelling, so the film can hold a roof and a frame for three days without ever filming inside anybody's house or making a household the subject.
what_to_film: Three matched shots from one fixed position directly overhead, at the same hour on three days: the old covering, the bare frame, the new covering. These three frames are the film.
The stripping in back-light and a little wind: armfuls of brittle grey material going over the edge, dust, an emptied roof space, the pole grid appearing a course at a time.
The bare frame from below at noon, with light coming straight down between the poles onto the floor, and the smoke-blackened undersides at arm's length.
The frame's joinery close: notches, bark still on the poles, old ties, the one or two poles that are visibly newer than the rest.
The making of the material on the ground: a frond split down its rib in one movement, leaflets flicked over one another, a stack of finished strips growing against a wall.
The tying at arm's length on the ladder: three turns and a hitch, and the next strip laid over the top edge so water cannot reach the tie.
The same course being worked by a fast pair of hands and a slow pair of hands, without comment.
The stripped covering in a heap and then burning in the yard, filmed as material and not as an event.
The first rain on the new covering, from underneath and from outside.
Wide from height once, so the belt reads: scattered homesteads, paddy, thorn, and how many of the roofs in view are leaf and how many are sheet.
suggested_location.access: By road from the district town. Everything depends on the household or institution whose building it is agreeing, and on being able to attach the film to a renewal already planned rather than asking for one; which means finding the work through somebody local who knows whose covering is due, and accepting the week the work happens in. This is dry-zone settlement country with elephant movement at night in places, so overnight positions and early starts have to be checked locally. Drone flight directly over a private compound needs the household's explicit agreement as well as any clearance required, and flying low enough for the three matched overhead frames must not be done while anybody is on the roof. The film should not be on a ladder or a roof at all.
suggested_location.best_time: A trusted dry stretch, because the work opens a building to the sky, which in practice means avoiding the north-east monsoon months and going when the belt itself says the coverings are being done. Within the day: mid-morning and mid-afternoon for the overhead frames, because a high sun rakes the courses and a low sun flattens them; noon for the bare frame; the last hour for the tying. The job is two or three days and cannot be compressed into one, and a return visit for the first rain on the new covering is worth planning separately.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, and unverified on the ground. From the sources above: woven coconut-palm leaf, known as cadjan, is a standard roofing and walling material of rural south Asia and Sri Lanka and is now largely confined to rural areas; thatch in Sri Lanka is described as being made from coconut fronds, coarse grass or palm leaf, and as requiring regular upkeep because it is vulnerable to pests, fire and moisture; and the town named in the coordinates is recorded as being in this district, about ten kilometres north of the district town on the road out of it. The coordinates are the published position of that town and are a direction towards the settlement belt around it, not a survey: no building, frame, covering, household, institution or working group has been identified or approached. The film's central assumptions are inferences and not confirmed facts about this belt: that coverings here are still stripped whole and re-laid rather than only patched, that the renewal interval is a few years, that the new material is made on site from local frond in the same week, and that outbuildings rather than dwellings are available as subjects. No specific renewal interval for this belt was found in any source and none should be quoted until somebody local gives one. No permission has been sought from any household or authority, and no photograph of thatching work, of a stripped frame or of this belt's roofs was found on Wikimedia Commons; the three images are of the covering type photographed abroad, of a leaf-roofed house generically, and of a village lane in this district.

unknowns: Whether whole coverings are still stripped to the frame and re-laid in this belt, or only patched, which decides whether the bare-frame shot exists.
What the renewal interval actually is here, and in which months the work is normally done.
Whether a renewal can be found and attached to inside a filming window, without any part of it being arranged.
Whether an outbuilding, cattle shelter or institutional roof is available, so that no dwelling's interior or occupants are filmed.
Whether a household will agree to a drone directly over their compound, and whether the three matched overhead frames can be flown safely around the work.
Whether the new material is still made on site from local frond, or bought in ready-plaited, which would remove one of the film's links.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is proposed by Claude from desk research and is unverified. No scene or shot is decided here.
